parts.title: DimCity PatchLab — a first look
parts.desc: Two minutes: the whole show, from patch to printed paperwork.
cues: Dim City Patch Lab. Everything between the lighting desk and the lamp, planned in one place.
Import your patch, and the whole show builds itself: every DB, every LK and Veam, every universe.
Build your racks and place them in the DB's. Every cable finds its socket and its node port by itself.
Nodes, switches and VLAN's are planned down to the last port.
Follow every universe through the signal flow, from the rack all the way to the lamp.
A clear plan always shows what is done and what comes next, so nobody on the team gets lost.
New: power distribution. Socapex cables, circuits and phases, with the amps worked out for you.
Then go live. Find every Lumi Node and Giga Core on the network, make them blink, and send the whole configuration at once.
And when it is done, the paperwork writes itself: reports, booklets, QR codes and stickers for every cable.
It speaks English and Dutch, and has a handbook and video guides built in, always one click away.
Dim City Patch Lab. Plan it. Patch it. Print it.

title: Build a show, step by step

parts.title: 1 · Import the patch
cues: Welcome to DimCity PatchLab. In this series we build a complete show from scratch: from the patch list to the finished PDF and the stickers.
This is an empty project. The device library of Luminex and ELC is already loaded, so you can start right away.
Everything starts with the patch list, a CSV file. Click Import CSV in the toolbar.
Choose which columns hold the LK or Veam ID, the port, the universe and the location. PatchLab detects them for you, and skips header and footer rows.
Click Import Selection.
The overview now shows three DB's with their LK blocks, Veams and universes, all taken from the file.
The patch list shows every row: LK's, Veams, loose DMX lines, and network cables, which start with the letter C.
The Validation page tells you what is wrong, such as a universe that is used twice, or a Veam that is not linked to an LK.
The Tasks page is your map. It shows the whole workflow as one line, and for every DB what is done and what comes next.
Below it is a square for every DB and every step. Click a square, and you go straight to the right place.
Setup walks through the same steps, with an explanation at every step. We use it in the next parts. Let's start with the racks.

parts.title: 2 · Racks and devices
parts.desc: Recorded before version 0.14: it still shows the advice card, which has been removed. Racks and devices are placed by hand now.
cues: Step two: racks and devices. Open a DB, here DB 1, and look at the card called Advice, best setup.
PatchLab counts the LK's, the Veams, the lines and the universes of this DB, and works out the best setup from the devices in your Device Builder.
It lists the panels and nodes it would use, how much rack space they take, and why. Here three nodes are enough, because a splitter would need more space.
It also advises a block mode per LK: twelve XLR for an LK with many ports, three Veams when an LK only carries Veams, and mixed in between. If an LK is set differently, one button fixes it.
Happy with it? Apply the advice. PatchLab adds a rack made for this DB, and a loose spider when only a few Veams do not deserve a whole panel.
You can always place racks and loose devices yourself, or change a rack in the Rack Builder. Setup brings you back to the same step afterwards.
Do the same for the other DB's. And FOH, front of house, where the lighting desk stands, is added with the plus next to the DimCities. It does not need a rack.

parts.title: 3 · Couple LKs and Veams
cues: Step three: couple the LK's and Veams to the sockets in the rack. Open DB 1 again.
By default everything is automatic. The LK's take the LK sockets in order, and the Veams fill the free Veam four sockets.
The table shows every LK and Veam, how many lines it has, the universes, and where it sits now.
Want it differently? Choose a socket yourself. For example, put LK one oh one on the second LK socket.
Or choose loose spider, when it should hang on a spider cable instead of a rack socket.
Or choose do not patch, to leave it out for now.
Your own choices are kept first, and everything else stays automatic. One button brings everything back to automatic.
A Veam that sits on a rack socket counts as patched. It no longer shows a warning that it is not linked to an LK.

parts.title: 4 · Nodes
cues: Step four: the nodes. The rack patch becomes the nodes and splitters of the network plan.
Click make the nodes in every DB. Every node gets its universes on the right ports, and later its port on the network switch.
Some DMX lines in the CSV say node two oh one dot one. That means DB 2, node 1, port 1.
Link automatically, and the universes of those lines are put on that node port.
You can also pick the name on the node itself, on the Nodes and Splitters page.

parts.title: 5 · Network
cues: Step five: the network. Every DB gets a network switch, and the nodes and the network cables take its ports in order.
First choose the numbering of the VLANs. Luminex style: management is VLAN one, group two is VLAN two hundred, and so on. Or use the FENT numbers.
Now add the switches. The Luminex GigaCore twenty T, three U set, is a special device, drawn exactly like the real one. DB 1 gets three of them.
The same switch in every other DB takes one click.
Open the Network page for the details. Switches and ports shows which port every node and cable takes, with the colour of its VLAN.
Before you are on site, plan the ports yourself. Pick a VLAN in the bar at the top, then drag across the ports of a switch. They take that VLAN.
Click a port to give it a name by hand. Without a name, the node or cable name is used. Later, Fill in from the plan puts all of it on the real switch.
On the VLAN tab you can rename any VLAN, change its colour, or add your own. The new name is used in the port plan, on the stickers and in the PDF.

parts.title: 6 · Fibres
cues: Step six: the fibres between the switches, inside a DB and between the DB's. First make your cable types in the Device Builder, on the Cables tab.
OpticalCON, FiberFox or SFP patch cables, each with a length. Half metres are fine, like seven point five.
On the Network page, on the Fibres tab, fill in how many of each cable you own.
Auto-assign chains the switches inside a DB with the short cable, and links the DB's with the long cable, as a ring. It only uses ports with the right connector.
A cable only fits ports with the same connector: opticalCON cable on opticalCON ports, FiberFox on FiberFox. Other ports are dimmed.
In the Signal Flow, under Show, choose Fibres. Every location is a card with its switches and fibre ports. Drag a switch by its name to place it next to another.
Cables run in straight lines and hop over each other with a little bridge. To draw one by hand, pick a cable at the bottom, click a free port, and then the port at the other end.

parts.title: 7 · Signal Flow
cues: The Signal Flow shows how the data runs from the rack to every object.
Hover a universe to follow it through the drawing. Click it to pin the route.
The Show switch shows everything, only DMX, only the network, or only the fibres.
Blocks never overlap. Drag a rack or a block to arrange it, and the arrangement is saved per DB. Auto layout puts everything back.
New: a background picture, like a floor plan or a stage plot. Choose a picture, then set the opacity, the size and the position.
It can be one picture for all the views, or its own picture for each view. Fit to drawing makes it cover everything.

parts.title: 8 · Check the plan
cues: Step seven of ten: check the plan. This is the last look at the plan on paper, before we touch the real devices. Look at the Tasks page first. When every square is green, the plan is complete.
In Setup, the check step lists the open issues, and links to the Signal Flow. Every step explains itself in three lines: what it is, what you do, and what comes next.

parts.title: 9 · Align the devices and send the configuration
cues: Steps eight and nine: the real devices. Open the Align tool from the Tasks page, or from Setup. Your devices must be switched on and connected to this computer.
Find searches the network for every Lumi Node and every Giga Core. It takes a few seconds.
Now align. One device blinks: a Giga Core blinks its screen and port lights, a Lumi Node its LED's. Go to the device that is blinking.
Press its place in the plan, for example DB one, switch one. The link is made, and the next device starts to blink. Orange is the suggestion.
You can skip a device, or undo the last link. When every device has its place, go on to send.
Fill in from the plan puts the names, the VLAN's, the port names and the universes on the devices. Nothing is sent yet.
Send config sends at once, with no extra question. Changing an IP address makes a device move, so do that on a new network.
When it is done, a window lists every change that was made, per device. Every device is read back and checked, so you know it really has the new settings.

parts.title: 10 · The P D F and the stickers
cues: The last step: print and share. Export PDF opens the report builder. Choose the sections: the patch, the racks, the signal flow, the network, the switch ports and the fibre links.
The QR codes section gives every DB a QR code that holds the whole DB as text, and the first page can carry one for the whole system.
A live preview shows every page before you export. Then export, and you have the report, ready to print or to send.
Stickers makes labels for Herma laser sheets: cable labels, panel strips, node ports, devices, switch ports, fibres and network cables.
Pick the Herma sheet, the DB, and what to print. The preview matches the sheet exactly, so you see what the printer will do.
Switch on DB info QR, and every DB gets stickers with a QR code that holds everything about that DB. The system QR does the same for the whole show.
A calibration sheet checks that your printer puts every label where the template says. And that is the whole workflow, from the CSV file to the printed show.

parts.title: Device Builder
parts.desc: Nodes, splitters, switches, panels and cables, with short names.
cues: The Device Builder holds every device you use: nodes, splitters, switches, panels, cables and racks. You open it from the Nodes and Splitters page.
Click Device Builder. Every kind of device has its own tab. Let's make a new node.
Give it a brand and a name, the number of DMX ports, and one or two Ethernet ports.
The short name is used in racks and overviews, so a long name is never cut off. Leave it empty, and PatchLab makes one for you.
On top, the preview shows the front of the device as it will look in a rack. Click Save node.
The new node is in the list, and in your own library, so it is there in every project. The same goes for splitters, switches and panels.
The button Fill short names, at the bottom, gives all your existing devices a short name at once, so you can adjust them afterwards.

parts.title: Rack Builder and custom racks
parts.desc: Build a rack from your devices, with or without an article key.
cues: Racks are built from your devices. Open the Device Builder on the Racks tab.
Click New rack, give it a name, and an article key if you use them. The key is optional.
Choose the height in units. A rack can never be lower than what is in it.
On the right are your devices. Click the plus to add one at the first free position, or drag it to the exact place you want.
Half width devices, like the LumiNode four, sit two side by side. Fill gaps adds black blind plates next to them.
The summary shows how much space is used. Close the builder, and place the rack in a DB.
Or build a rack right here: Custom rack. Choose how many panels, nodes, splitters and switches it holds, and PatchLab places them. No article key is needed.
Click Build and place, and the rack is in the DB, with its own name, and the LK and the lines of this DB are patched onto it.

parts.title: Couple LKs to sockets, and stack racks
parts.desc: Choose the socket of every LK and Veam, and tell PatchLab which racks stand on top of each other.
cues: Every LK and Veam needs a socket. Open a DB, and find the table Couple LK's and Veams to sockets.
Automatic fills the sockets in order. Or choose a socket yourself, a loose spider, or do not patch.
One button returns everything to automatic.
Now an important rule. LK and Veam cables are short. A socket in one rack can only feed nodes in the same rack. Here the panels are in one rack, and the nodes in another.
Only network cables can run from rack to rack. Two racks that stand directly on top of each other count as one: that is the tick, stacked on the rack above.
Without that tick, the LK's have no node in their own rack. PatchLab warns, and offers a Fix button.
Press Fix, and the racks are stacked. Everything is patched again.
A node without a rack always comes with a spider. Add a loose node, and an LK spider is added with it, because a loose node has no panel to be fed from.

parts.title: Cable types, fibre stock and auto-assign
parts.desc: Make fibre cable types, enter your stock, and let PatchLab link the switches.
cues: Fibres start with cable types. Open the Device Builder on the Cables tab.
A cable type has a medium, a number of cores, a connector at both ends, and a length. Half metres are fine, like seven point five.
OpticalCON, FiberFox and SFP patch cables each have their own connector. A cable only fits ports with the same connector. Click save.
On the Network page, on the Fibres tab, enter how many of each cable you own. The stock is counted for you.
Auto-assign chains the switches inside a DB with the short cable, and links the DB's with the long cable, as a ring or a chain.
It tells you if the stock is not enough, and which connectors are missing. Press Assign, and the links are made.
The list shows every fibre, with its two ends. Remove one, and the cable goes back into the stock.

parts.title: The fibre overview
parts.desc: See and draw the fibres in the Signal Flow.
cues: The fibre overview is in the Signal Flow. Open it, and under Show, choose Fibres.
Every location is a card with its switches. Each switch shows its fibre ports with their number and connector.
Zoom with the wheel, or the buttons. Drag the background to move around.
Drag a switch by its name. It moves live, and its cables follow, so you can place it exactly where it belongs.
Cables run in straight lines, and hop over each other with a little bridge.
To draw a cable by hand, pick a cable type at the bottom, click a free port, and then the port at the other end. Ports with the wrong connector are dimmed.
Click a cable to select it, and remove it with the button. Auto-assign and the stock are right here too.

parts.title: VLANs and addresses
parts.desc: Rename VLANs, change colours, add your own, and see the port plan.
cues: Everything about the network is on the Network page. Switches and ports shows what every port of a switch is used for.
Every port has the colour of its VLAN, so you see at a glance which network a cable belongs to.
The VLAN tab lists all VLANs. Choose Luminex numbering, or the FENT scheme.
Click a name to rename a VLAN, and change its colour. The new name is used in the port plan, on the stickers and in the PDF.
Add your own VLAN with a number and a name. It can be removed again, and a standard VLAN can be reset to its standard name.
The Overview tab shows every device with its addresses, and warns about addresses that are used twice.

parts.title: The Signal Flow
parts.desc: Follow the data from the rack to every object, with layers and a background picture.
cues: The Signal Flow shows how the data runs from the rack to every object, for all DB's or one at a time.
Hover a universe in the list to follow it through the drawing. Click it to pin the route.
Hover a port or a line, and everything on that route lights up. Escape lets go.
The Show switch chooses the layer: everything, only DMX, only the network, or only the fibres.
Drag a block to arrange the drawing. Blocks never overlap, and the arrangement is saved per DB. Auto layout puts everything back.
A background picture, like a floor plan or a stage plot, goes under the drawing. Choose a picture, then set the opacity, the size and the position.
Save image exports the drawing as a picture, and Share image copies it, for example to send in a chat.

parts.title: The PDF report builder
parts.desc: Choose the sections, order and style of the report.
cues: Export PDF opens the report builder. On the left you choose what goes in, on the right a live preview shows every page.
Every section can be switched on or off: the DB header, network, splitters, racks, signal flow, patch, universes, the patch list, warnings and notes.
Drag a section by its handle to change the order. Racks has options: the rack drawing, node ports, loose devices and the patch table.
The new QR codes section puts QR codes on the page that hold the whole DB as text, and optionally the whole system.
Style, header and footer, cover page and logo are set in the other tabs. Save the layout as a template, and use it again in the next project.
Choose one PDF with all DB's, or one file per DB. Then export.

parts.title: Stickers for Herma sheets
parts.desc: Print cable labels, strips, device labels and more on laser sheets.
cues: Stickers prints labels on Herma laser sheets. Click Stickers in the toolbar.
Choose the sheet. The preview shows the sheet exactly as the printer will print it.
Choose what to print: cable labels, panel connection labels, node ports, racks and devices, fibres, network cables and switch ports.
Every sticker has the colour of its node, so you can see where a cable goes. Cables get two labels, one for each end.
If the sheet is already partly used, set the first label to start with, and use the rest.
The calibration sheet prints outlines only. Print it on a real sheet and hold it to the light, to check that every label sits where the template says.

parts.title: QR codes for a DB and the system
parts.desc: Scan one QR code and see everything about a D B.
cues: A QR code can hold much more than a cable name. Open a DB, and look at the card At a glance.
At a glance shows the LK blocks with their socket and node, the racks and their devices, the nodes and splitters, and the network switches with their fibres.
Click the QR button. These QR codes hold all of this as plain text. Scan them with any phone camera, and you can read it.
A long DB is cut into numbered parts. Scan them in order. You can copy the text, or save the codes as an SVG file.
The same codes can be printed. In Stickers, switch on DB info QR and system QR, and every DB gets its own set.
And in the PDF report, the QR codes section puts them on the page of each DB. The system code is on the first page.

parts.title: Exchange with Lightwright and Vectorworks
parts.desc: Send the patch to another program and take their changes back.
cues: PatchLab can exchange the patch with Lightwright and Vectorworks, in both directions. Open the Tasks page, and click Open exchange.
Choose the program. Export writes a file with one row per LK or Veam port: the circuit name, the position, and the universe.
Import that file in Lightwright or Vectorworks, and match on the circuit name. The note under the button tells you where.
After you changed things there, export the same list again, and choose it here with Choose file.
PatchLab matches every row, and shows what differs: universe, or position. Everything else is left alone.
Tick the changes you want, and press Apply. They are written into the patch, and validation runs again.
Rows that exist only in the file can be added as new lines. Rows that exist only in PatchLab are counted, but never removed.

parts.title: Network config
parts.desc: Find the devices, paint the V L A N's on the ports, change any setting, and send it.
cues: Network Config holds all your Lumi Nodes and Giga Core switches on one page. Open it from the Tasks page. The Align tool next to it is for setting up many devices in one go.
Discover devices looks at the whole network and lists every Lumi Node and Giga Core. Each one is linked to its place in the plan.
Open a switch. Its ports are tiles, as on the front panel, each with its number, name and VLAN.
To set VLAN's, pick a VLAN as the brush, then click ports or drag over them. They get that VLAN, like in Araneo.
Click a port without a brush to change its name, its VLAN, the P o E and the speed.
All settings lists everything the device lets you change, in sections, with a search box. A column header has an all button to set one value on every row.
Send to other devices copies your changes, or whole sections, to as many devices of the same kind as you tick. Only the differences are prepared.
Apply sends at once. Afterwards the device is read back, and a window lists exactly what was changed.

parts.title: Power: P D's and Socapex
parts.desc: Build your P D's, load the fixture sheet, and see the amps on every phase.
cues: The Power page is a part of its own. It works from the fixture sheet, so you can use it without the rest of the project.
Import the fixture sheet, the CSV from Vectorworks or Lightwright. Its circuit name is a Socapex cable, the circuit number is one to six, and the wattage gives the amps.

Under PD types you build your distros, like node types. Choose the input, and add Socapex, Han sixteen, CEE and Schuko outputs. A multi output has its own circuits, the phase it starts on, and an amp limit. Examples are one click away.
Under PD's and feeds, add a feed, a Powerlock run with its maximum current, and add the PD's of this DB.
Fill cables automatically gives every PD a block of twelve cable numbers, in order, as Soca A, B, C and so on. You can also choose a cable per Socapex yourself.
The overview shows every PD and feed with the amps on L one, L two and L three. Yellow and red warn you when a feed gets heavy, or a circuit goes over sixteen amps.
Open a PD, and you see it like a page of the booklet. Every Socapex has six circuits, with the DMX, the fixture numbers, what hangs there, the location, and the amps on the phase.
Booklet makes the PDF: a cover, the overview per DB, a page per PD, and the power summary.

parts.title: Tasks and Setup
parts.desc: Always know what is done and what comes next.
cues: You always know what comes next. The Tasks page shows the whole workflow, from the patch to the printed show.
On top is the next thing to do, with a button that takes you there. The line shows the ten steps, done in green.
Below, every DB has a square for every step. Orange is still to do, yellow needs attention, green is done.
Click Do this now. Setup opens on the right step, for the right DB.
Setup explains each step in a few lines, shows what is done, and lets you skip a step. Nothing is locked.
The progress bar at the bottom left shows how complete the show is. Click it for the checklist, with a jump to the place where it is solved.
And on the Overview page, a short bar shows the next step too, so you never have to search.

parts.title: Search, undo and saving
parts.desc: Find anything, undo mistakes, and keep your work safe.
cues: Search finds anything in the show: an LK, a Veam, a universe, a location or a node. Click Search, or press command K.
Type a few letters, and the results appear at once. Press enter to open one.
Every change can be undone. The history lists what you did in plain words, so you can go back to a moment before a mistake.
Save writes the project to a file. PatchLab also keeps back-ups, and recovers your work after a crash.
Help opens the manual for the page you are on, with these videos. And Request sends a wish or a bug to the developer.
